extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how journalists should attribute material taken from press releases, balancing accuracy, PR expectations, and newsroom ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution for direct quotes, facts, or figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution is “recommended” when journalists use direct quotes, facts or figures from press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Gerard Corbett (PRSA), journalists should attribute direct quotes and factual data drawn from a release; this is framed as a recommended ethical practice rather than a legal necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No attribution required for dates, times, or general information
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution is not required when using dates, times or other general information from press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine factual details (e.g., event dates/times, general locational info) can be used without attribution according to the guidance cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using verbatim press-release text can improve accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulling content verbatim from the press release can be a way to insure a story’s accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes press releases often undergo a meticulous drafting/editing/review process intended to present a client’s news correctly; quoting verbatim may preserve that intended accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand PR intentions — they want publication and message delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations professionals like seeing their releases published and view publication as delivering key messages for their companies or clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that PR practitioners generally welcome publication of their copy, which may factor into newsroom decisions about attribution and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of potential scrutiny and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists face scrutiny and criticism over the practice of publishing press-release content without attribution despite PR acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although PRSA frames non-attribution as not plagiarism, newsrooms should weigh reputational risks and audience expectations; the piece promises practical troubleshooting ('six ways') to address attribution concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRSA position: using release material without attribution is not plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerard Corbett, chair and CEO of the Public Relations Society of America, says using a press release without attribution isn’t plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the professional association's stance — a normative claim differentiating ethical recommendation (attribution advised in many cases) from an accusation of plagiarism.
